claim: Si, Hashimoto and Yang ran 43 experts who each executed a randomly assigned LLM or human idea; LLM ideas lost significantly more review score after execution on novelty, excitement, effectiveness and overall, closing the ideation-stage gap.
quote: Each expert spent over 100 hours implementing the idea and wrote a 4-page short paper to document the experiments.
authors: Chenglei Si, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Diyi Yang
title: The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
transfer: Do not trust paper-stage novelty of generated ideas; add a cheap execution or prior-art check before selecting an idea on open tasks.

claim: The Si 2025 execution study is listed as an ICLR 2026 poster, so it passed peer review, but no independent replication by a different team turned up in this search round.
quote: a good idea should not simply appear to be novel, it should also result in better research after being executed.
authors: Chenglei Si, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Diyi Yang
title: The Ideation-Execution Gap
venue: ICLR 2026 poster page seen in search result

claim: CHECK: The claim that the LLM novelty edge vanishes after execution is still single-team, single-pool evidence (Si et al.). The only other execution-related paper found is a proxy benchmark, not an execution test. Verdict: still single-source, treat as hypothesis. Web search budget ran out in this round, so absence of replication is not proven.
quote: do not substitute for expert review or execution-grounded validation
title: Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation
transfer: Test the execution flip on our own architecture search: compare idea-stage score with measured perplexity.

claim: On a noisy pool of LLM research ideas, refining only a diversity-selected subset (MMR-k) gave the best proxy tradeoff and the lowest duplicate rate; random-k refinement was a strong cheap baseline; uniform refinement of all was not the best use of compute.
quote: diversity-aware MMR-k refinement gives the best overall proxy tradeoff
title: Budgeted Subset Refinement for Execution-Aware LLM Research Ideation
transfer: After generating N ideas, dedupe and pick a diverse subset of k to refine, rather than refining all or the judge's top few.

claim: A humor-generation system with best-of-N writing, self-critique and LLM judging tied a plain Gemini 2.5 Flash baseline; the authors say elaborate scaffolding gives diminishing returns with strong frontier models. One task, small English test.
quote: elaborate prompt engineering and agentic scaffolding yield diminishing returns with strong frontier models
authors: Marek Suppa, Viktoria Ondrejova, Lucia Ganajova, Gregor Karetka, Daniel Skala
title: RAGthoven at SemEval-2026 Task 1
transfer: Measure whether extra scaffold stages beat plain sampling on each open task before keeping them.

claim: CHECK: No source found that gives a curve of how many LLM ideas to generate before returns diminish, with an external selector versus an LLM judge. Searches for best-of-N creativity returned nothing relevant. Verdict: gap stays open; only Tian 2024 (one point) and our own runs can set N.
title: gap check, best-of-N creative scaling
transfer: Run our own N sweep (N=4,8,16,32) on NoveltyBench with an external dedupe selector and report distinct answers per N.

claim: Self-correction helps open-ended generation through re-interpretation and compositional refinement, while multiple-choice selection has clearer boundaries but is limited by the options given. Design should account for task structure.
quote: open-ended generation often benefits from the flexibility of re-interpretation and compositional refinement
authors: Hossein A. Rahmani, Satyapriya Krishna, Xi Wang, Mohammadmehdi Naghiaei, Emine Yilmaz
title: Self-Correcting Large Language Models: Generation vs. Multiple Choice
n: various tasks and model families, counts not on abstract page
transfer: Gate reflection by task type: allow revision loops on open generation, skip or restrict them when the answer is a pick from fixed options.

claim: On an open-ended but rule-constrained task, eight frontier models gained little from self-critique, repeated the same violations, and did worse as open-endedness rose. Gains came from chance, not error detection. External constraint checking is needed.
quote: Performance before and after reflection deteriorates as open-endedness increases
authors: Sion Weatherhead, Flora Salim, Aaron Belbasis
title: Illusions of reflection: open-ended task reveals systematic failures in Large Language Models' reflective reasoning
transfer: Reflection on open tasks needs a program-run checker of explicit constraints, not model self-critique alone.

claim: CHECK: Tension between 'always-doubt helped open tasks' (our data) and 'reflection fails when open-ended' (Weatherhead 2025). Verdict: partly reconciled. Ours rewards diversity of answers, theirs rewards constraint validity. Reflection can widen output but not fix rule violations. Rahmani 2025 supports task-structure gating. Both are preprints.
quote: the second attempt frequently repeats the same violation of constraint
authors: Weatherhead et al.; Rahmani et al.
title: synthesis of arXiv 2510.18254 and 2511.09381
transfer: Use forced divergence for spread, and a separate external checker for hard constraints. Gate by: open and unconstrained, open and constrained, single-answer.

claim: An analogical-retrieval framework (Idea-Catalyst) that reframes a goal as domain-agnostic problems and retrieves from other disciplines reports average novelty up 21 percent and insightfulness up 16 percent. The abstract does not say whether humans or an LLM judged.
quote: this targeted integration improves average novelty by 21% and insightfulness by 16%
authors: Priyanka Kargupta, Shuhaib Mehri, Dilek Hakkani-Tur, Jiawei Han
title: Sparking Scientific Creativity via LLM-Driven Interdisciplinary Inspiration
transfer: Add a step: restate the problem without domain words, recall distant-field solutions, then map back. Test with execution outcomes, not novelty ratings.

claim: A benchmark of 2,061 creative puzzles needing facts from different domains found models score lower than on factual questions, often recalling the right knowledge but failing to make the non-obvious connection.
authors: Mete Ismayilzada, Renqing Cuomao, Daniil Yurshevich, Anna Sotnikova, Lonneke van der Plas, Antoine Bosselut
title: CresOWLve: Benchmarking Creative Problem-Solving Over Real-World Knowledge
transfer: Retrieval of the right fact is not the bottleneck; add an explicit connect-the-two-facts step and test it.

claim: CHECK: No controlled study with human or execution outcomes of distant-domain analogical retrieval for LLM problem solving was found (Gentner and Dunbar not located in this round either). Only LLM-rated or benchmark evidence. Verdict: gap open; analogy step stays a hypothesis.
title: gap check, analogical retrieval
transfer: Run an A/B on architecture search: with versus without a distant-analogy step, judged by measured perplexity.

claim: Huang and Xie argue that small teams' disruption edge is a measurement artefact: the standard disruption index falls mechanically as reference lists lengthen, larger teams cite more (about 60 million papers), and a reference-robust version shows disruption rising with team size.
quote: the standard disruption index declines mechanically as reference lists lengthen
title: Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
transfer: none for a single agent; warns against treating small-team disruption as a design rule.

claim: Lin, Li and Wu (Wu 2019 team) report the negative link between team size and disruption holds after controlling for reference length, citation impact and period; a 5-year window can make it look positive; small-team impact may take a decade.
quote: Like 'sleeping beauties,' small teams need a decade or more to see their transformative contributions to science.
authors: Yiling Lin, Linzhuo Li, Lingfei Wu
title: Team Size and Its Negative Impact on the Disruption Index
n: earlier work: 65 million projects across papers, patents and software

claim: Petersen, Arroyave and Pammolli find the disruption index drops partly through longer reference lists; the team-size relationship is weak in magnitude and turns positive at 8 or more coauthors.
quote: the negative relationship between disruption and team-size is remarkably small in overall magnitude
authors: Alexander M. Petersen, Felber Arroyave, Fabio Pammolli
title: The disruption index suffers from citation inflation and is confounded by shifts in scholarly citation practice

claim: CHECK: Wu, Wang, Evans 2019 'small teams disrupt'. Verdict: contested, not refuted. Original authors defend it with controls (Lin 2025); independent critics show reference-list artefacts and effect reversal (Petersen 2024, Huang and Xie 2026). I found no zero-reference-specific correction; the Huang and Xie abstract does not mention zero references. All three are preprints. Do not use as a design rule.
quote: Evaluating each paper against one reference at a time yields a reference-robust measure
authors: Huang and Xie; Lin, Li and Wu; Petersen et al.
title: synthesis

claim: Unusual pairings of datasets in 30,000+ social science papers (5,000+ ICPSR datasets) are linked to higher scientific and public impact even after controlling for topic atypicality; smaller, less experienced teams do it more; it stays rare. Partial extension of Uzzi to datasets, but no conventional-core test seen in the abstract.
quote: combining datasets, particularly those infrequently paired, significantly contributes to both scientific and broader impacts
title: Does the Use of Unusual Combinations of Datasets Contribute to Greater Scientific Impact?
transfer: Unusual pairings of ingredients pay off in one more setting; supports a small share of unusual pairings in a mix.

claim: CHECK: Uzzi 2013 conventional core plus atypical tail. Verdict: still no replication in patents, software or LLM ideas that tests the conventional-core part. Yu and Romero 2024 supports the atypical part only, in datasets. The patents query returned only irrelevant patent filings and the web search budget then ran out. Remains single-source for the core-plus-tail rule; keep as a hypothesis to test.
title: gap check, Uzzi replication
transfer: Test in our loop: mostly standard architecture plus one or two unusual changes versus all-unusual.
